title: Personalization Without Stereotyping: Do Speech LLMs Know When to Turn a Deaf Ear?

paper.title: Personalization Without Stereotyping: Do Speech LLMs Know When to Turn a Deaf Ear?
paper.abstract:
Abstract Recent speech LLMs can leverage rich paralinguistic cues, enabling more complex and personalized interactions. However, little work investigates how this sensitivity can lead to stereotyping, and existing evaluations largely measure demographic disparities without distinguishing beneficial personalization from stereotypical behavior. We introduce BASIS-Bench , a benchmark designed
to disentangle these two aspects through three axes: (1) demographic robustness , measuring disparities in content-based tasks across speakers and demographic classification capabilities; (2) stereotypical bias , measuring whether perceived demographic cues trigger unprompted stereotypical behavior; and (3) personalization , measuring whether models can tailor responses to demographic characteristics when explicitly requested.
We evaluate eight recent speech LLMs and find that, despite often recognizing demographic cues, most fail to translate them into appropriate personalization. Explicit demographic labels improve personalization but also amplify stereotypical associations already present in the textual backbones.
These findings highlight the need to train speech LLMs not only to perceive demographic cues, but to learn when they should shape their responses.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Speech LLMs are increasingly capable of leveraging not only linguistic content but also information conveyed by the speaker’s voice, enabling more natural and personalized interactions. In particular, speech provides demographic cues such as age and gender that are unavailable from linguistic content alone. This creates a new challenge: a capable speech assistant should exploit these cues when appropriate, while ignoring them when they are irrelevant or could lead to unfair, stereotypical, or otherwise inappropriate behavior. Personalization and stereotypical bias are therefore not independent phenomena, but two outcomes of the same underlying sensitivity to speaker characteristics, distinguished by whether demographic cues are used when relevant or irrelevant to the task. Yet, existing speech LLMs evaluations do not always cleanly disentangle these aspects. Bias benchmarks typically assess demographic disparities under controlled linguistic content, encompassing stereotypical bias towards demographic groups [ 28 ] as well as performance and recommendation disparities [ 45 ] . Meanwhile, some personalization and paralinguistic-aware benchmarks reward demographic-dependent changes in model responses even when such adaptation is not explicitly requested by the user [ 2 , 49 ] . 1 1 1 For instance, ParaS2S rewards gender-tailored responses without an explicit request for personalization; SD-Eval rewards mimicking the speaker’s accent without such a request. Thus, similar demographic-dependent behavior may be rewarded as personalization or penalized as stereotyping across evaluations. Motivated by Kantharuban et al. [26] , we distinguish these outcomes by considering demographic personalization desirable only when explicitly requested. Building on this distinction, we introduce BASIS-Bench ( B ias A nd per S onalization I n S peech LLMs Bench mark). We define three evaluation axes: (1) demographic robustness , measuring disparities in content-related tasks across speakers and demographic classification capabilities; (2) stereotypical bias , measuring whether perceived demographic cues trigger stereotypical behavior when they are irrelevant to the task; and (3) personalization , measuring whether models can tailor responses to demographic characteristics when explicitly requested. To characterize the sources of demographic-dependent behavior along these axes, we further distinguish three potential effects: the acoustic effect , arising from speech encoding; the backbone effect , inherited from the underlying language model; and the interaction effect , arising from their interaction. Together, this framework allows us to isolate different sources of demographic disparity and distinguish failures to process speech and perceive demographic information from its appropriate or inappropriate use. Our results show that recent speech LLMs achieve similar content-based task performance across demographic groups and often correctly identify speakers’ demographic characteristics. Yet, consistent with previous work [ 49 ] , most models show limited personalization across age and gender when demographic information must be inferred from speech. Providing them explicitly via text substantially improves personalization, suggesting that these failures primarily reflect difficulty translating speech demographic cues into appropriate behavior changes rather than an inability to personalize. Conversely, models consistently exhibit stereotypical behavior toward female and elderly speakers. This behavior is amplified by explicit demographic information but persists when speech is replaced by its transcription, suggesting that much of it originates in the backbone rather than from the use of speech. Together, these findings suggest that speech LLMs are not yet reliable at deciding when and how demographic information should shape their behavior: they struggle to turn perceived demographic cues into appropriate personalization, yet readily reproduce stereotypes when such information is irrelevant. Our contributions are the following: (1) We introduce BASIS-Bench to disentangle stereotypical bias from personalization while diagnosing three potential sources of demographic-dependent behavior: acoustic, backbone, and interaction effects. (2) We release data resources, including Spoken StereoSet+ , a manually filtered version of the original dataset [ 28 ] with explicit definitions of stereotypical bias and associated harms; ELIP-Pair , an age personalization dataset based on ELIP [ 42 ] ; and BASIS-Health and BASIS-Product , synthetic gender personalization datasets. (3) We provide a comprehensive evaluation of eight popular speech LLMs across demographic robustness, stereotypical bias, and personalization, revealing systematic gaps in how models perceive and use demographic information.

sections.heading: Speech LLMs
sections.text: Following the success of text-only LLMs, numerous speech-native assistants have been proposed for end-to-end spoken interaction, progressively expanding from modeling linguistic content, to jointly modeling acoustic and paralinguistic information such as speaker identity, prosody, emotion, and speaking style [ 39 , 14 , 25 , 46 , 47 , 44 , 15 , 31 , 48 , 32 , 21 , 22 ] . This evolution reflects the growing recognition that effective spoken language interaction requires modeling both linguistic content and acoustic characteristics.

sections.heading: Bias in Speech Systems
sections.text: Bias evaluation in speech systems has been extensively studied in recent years [ 13 , 20 , 18 , 8 , 12 , 33 , 34 , 30 , 43 , 3 , 16 , 24 , 23 ] . We highlight that while speech LLMs are subject to the same sources of demographic disparity as single-purpose systems (e.g., transcription and translation systems), their broader capabilities introduce additional ways in which demographics can affect model behavior. Assessing disparities arising from speech encoding alone is therefore insufficient to capture their potential harms.

sections.heading: Data for Speech LLM Bias Evaluation
sections.text: The majority of existing bias datasets for speech LLMs are repurposed from existing textual datasets [ 28 , 29 , 11 ] . Consequently, most evaluate bias primarily through lexical content rather than on acoustic features and their interaction. For example, Choi et al. [11] resynthesize contexts from the text-based BBQ dataset [ 37 ] , thus stereotypical associations are primarily encoded in lexical rather than acoustic cues. We argue that this approach fails to capture the modality-specific biases embedded in end-to-end speech LLMs. A more compelling evaluation protocol must investigate how model behavior shifts in response to demographic information conveyed through speech. Datasets where semantic content remains fixed, but the speaker’s acoustic attributes vary thus provide a more realistic measure of bias in speech LLMs [ 28 , 45 ] .

sections.heading: Personalization
sections.text: Recent speech LLM benchmarks such as SD-Eval [ 2 ] , ParaS2S [ 49 ] , and EchoMind [ 51 ] evaluate whether speech LLMs can leverage paralinguistic cues for generating speaker-aware responses, covering cues such as emotion, accent, age, gender, sarcasm, and environmental sounds. SD-Eval and EchoMind take broader approaches spanning multiple paralinguistic and reasoning capabilities, while ParaS2S focuses on speaker traits through incongruent speech scenarios where linguistic content alone cannot determine the appropriate response. Overall, these works show that current models have substantial room for improvement in leveraging paralinguistic cues. In parallel, recent work in the textual domain has investigated to what extent LLMs can derive implicit demographic cues from the user interaction and provide unprompted personalization. Kantharuban et al. [26] show that LLM recommendations can be influenced by explicit or implicit racial identity, producing stereotypical recommendations even when personalization is not requested, while Entezami and Endres [17] find that demographic attributes unrelated to the task can influence AI-assisted software development outputs. In this work, we focus on speech LLMs, jointly evaluating their ability to reliably perceive demographic cues, personalize based on them when requested, and avoid unprompted stereotypical behavior.

sections.heading: 3 BASIS-Bench
sections.text: We introduce BASIS-Bench ( B ias A nd per S onalization I n S peech LLMs Bench mark), a benchmark designed to disentangle personalization from stereotypical bias in speech LLMs and diagnose the factors underlying demographic-dependent disparities. Focusing primarily on age and gender, we first introduce three complementary evaluation axes (§ 3.1 - 3.3 ), then define a framework that disentangles the sources of demographic disparity along them (§ 3.4 ). Figure 1 provides an overview, and Appendix B describes additional inference and evaluation settings. Figure 1: Overview of BASIS-Bench : evaluation axes, tasks, demographic dimensions, and datasets.

sections.heading: 3.1 Demographic Robustness Axis
sections.text: We use demographic robustness to assess whether speech LLMs can reliably process and perceive speech across speakers with diverse demographic characteristics. We evaluate two complementary capabilities: whether models can perceive demographic cues through age and gender classification, and whether they exhibit performance disparities across speakers on content-based tasks, namely automatic speech recognition (ASR) and spoken question answering (SQA). Together, these evaluations provide context for interpreting the subsequent stereotypical bias and personalization axes by establishing whether models can reliably process speech and perceive demographic cues.

sections.heading: Data
sections.text: For ASR, we use Fair-Speech [ 43 ] , Spoken StereoSet+ (ASR Age Split), and SD-QA [ 18 ] . 2 2 2 While our demographic dimensions are age and gender, we additionally consider accent for ASR/SQA to broaden our robustness assessment across diverse speakers. Fair-Speech covers different genders and accents; we do not use its age labels, which span 18-65 years and therefore do not cover children or elderly speakers. We use the Spoken StereoSet+ ASR Age Split (Appendix A.1.3 ) to assess performance across age groups; we describe its construction in § 3.2 . SD-QA covers different accents and it is also used for SQA, while LibriSQA [ 50 ] assesses SQA performance across gender categories. For demographic classification, we use the same data as the other axes, enabling direct comparisons across axes.

sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.text: For ASR, we report word error rate (WER) between the gold and generated transcripts after applying the Whisper normalizer [ 38 ] . We cap WER at 100 and report accuracy ( 100 − WER 100-\mathrm{WER} ) averaged for each demographic (accent, gender, and age) and dataset (SD-QA, Fair-Speech, Spoken StereoSet+). For SQA we use LLM-as-judge evaluation, computing mean accuracy for each demographic category (accent and gender) and dataset (SD-QA and LibriSQA) before aggregating across them. We then average the resulting ASR and SQA scores to obtain the context-based score for each model. For demographic classification, we explicitly provide the possible categories in the evaluation prompt, reducing the task to implicit MCQA, and reporting exact-match accuracy per-label. We then average across labels, obtaining the final classification score.

sections.heading: 3.2 Stereotypical Bias Axis
sections.text: We use stereotypical bias to refer to harmful forms of stereotyping, where a demographic group is associated with particular characteristics, attributes, or behaviors, and these associations are used to draw unwarranted inferences about individual members [ 7 , 4 ] . In speech LLMs, this can manifest when speech demographic cues, such as gender or age, influence a model’s response based on stereotypical assumptions about a speaker’s characteristics, preferences, abilities, or social roles. Such behavior can reinforce social stereotypes and lead to differential treatment across speakers with equivalent requests. This axis thus assesses whether models exhibit stereotypical behavior based on perceived demographic cues when their use is not explicitly requested. 3 3 3 We provide a discussion of stereotyping, its relationship to bias, and the harms considered in this work in Appendix A.1.1 .

sections.heading: Data
sections.text: We build on Spoken StereoSet [ 28 ] , introducing a manual filtering stage to align the dataset with our definition of stereotypical bias for age and gender. We consider adult and elderly male speakers for age, and female and male speakers for gender. We detail our definitions and post-processing in Appendix A.1 , and refer to the resulting dataset as Spoken StereoSet+ .

sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.text: We follow the context association test (CAT) from StereoSet [ 36 ] , reporting the proportions of stereotypical and anti-stereotypical continuations. Since irrelevant continuations are negligible, 4 4 4 All models select irrelevant examples in < 2 % <2\% of cases, except DeSTA2.5 for which this rate goes up to 11%. we omit them for brevity. To mitigate positional bias in the MCQA setting [ 40 ] , we evaluate all answer-option permutations and report mean accuracy for both stereotypical and anti-stereotypical continuations. We additionally adopt the idealized CAT (ICAT) score from StereoSet, which jointly captures continuation relevance and the skew between stereotypical and anti-stereotypical choices. ICAT ranges from 0 (maximally biased) to 100 (unbiased). We report the per-demographic mean ICAT score as a single number measuring bias per model, rather than an overall ICAT, to prevent opposing stereotypical and anti-stereotypical behaviors across demographics from balancing out and producing an apparent unbiased score.

sections.heading: 3.3 Personalization Axis
sections.text: This axis assesses whether models can use demographic information conveyed through a speaker’s voice to tailor their responses. A key challenge is determining when such adaptation is appropriate, as inferring preferences from age or gender can itself constitute stereotyping. Motivated by Kantharuban et al. [26] , we thus consider personalization appropriate only when explicitly requested. For age personalization , we focus on developmental differences between children and adults, adapting the complexity, style, or presentation of information based on cognitive development differences rather than socially constructed stereotypes. We do not treat elderly speakers as a separate personalization category, as defining age-based adaptations for this group would require assumptions about their cognitive abilities or needs that may themselves be stereotypical. Instead, the adult category spans young to elderly adult speakers. During inference, the model receives a spoken question along with textual descriptions of the adult and child profiles and is asked to answer in the same style as the speaker’s demographic profile. For gender personalization , we similarly find that existing formulations are difficult to disentangle from stereotypical bias. We thus formulate it as a constrained gender recognition task: when explicitly instructed to personalize based on the speaker’s voice, the model must select the only response containing the speaker’s gender marker. We introduce two datasets: BASIS-Health , covering health questions whose answers depend on biological sex, 5 5 5 See Limitations regarding our sex/gender labels. and BASIS-Product , covering product recommendations where identical options differ by the gender marker (e.g., Men’s vs. Women’s razor). These datasets assess whether models exploit gender information when explicitly requested , while minimizing reliance on stereotypical associations.

sections.heading: Data
sections.text: For age personalization, we follow Thonet et al. [42] and create and manually validate an expanded version of ELIP, ELIP-Pair , containing 521 questions, each associated with two responses tailored to distinct personas: child and adult. We synthesize child and adult speech by cloning other synthetic voices, and then automatically filtering the result based on both ASR quality and age classification. Outliers are then manually verified. For gender personalization, we create BASIS-Health and BASIS-Product using Claude-Opus, followed by GPT-5.6 filtering, speech synthesis, and similar automatic and manual post-processing from ELIP-Pair. Detailed generation pipelines for these datasets are provided in Appendix A.2 and § A.3 .

sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.text: For gender personalization, we report per-demographic accuracy and, as for stereotypical bias, we evaluate all answer-option permutations to mitigate positional bias. For age personalization, we classify the response as child- or adult-oriented using LLM-as-judge.

sections.heading: 3.4 Disparity Sources and Evaluation Modes
sections.text: Although bias in speech systems is well studied [ 30 , 43 ] and textual LLMs have been extensively evaluated for demographic bias [ 36 , 37 ] , existing evaluations of speech LLMs lack a systematic framework for distinguishing whether demographic-dependent behavior originates from the speech encoder, the backbone, or their interaction. We therefore distinguish three sources of demographic disparity, and design our evaluation framework to disentangle their contributions. The acoustic effect originates from disparities in the speech encoding process, where speaker characteristics may affect how reliably linguistic content or demographic cues are represented and perceived. For example, strongly accented or non-standard dialectal speech may be less reliably processed than speech varieties overrepresented in training data, resulting in performance gaps. The backbone effect refers to biases and personalization capabilities inherited from the language model, independently of the speech modality. Recent work has shown that LLMs can infer demographic characteristics from implicit cues and exhibit demographic stereotypes and disparate treatment across sensitive attributes [ 36 , 35 , 41 , 26 ] . A speech LLM may therefore inherit tendencies such as occupational gender stereotypes or culturally skewed recommendations, from its backbone. The interaction effect arises from the interaction between speech representations and the backbone. Even when speech is faithfully encoded, demographic and other paralinguistic cues may introduce demographic-dependent behavior or amplify or attenuate biases already present in the backbone. This effect captures how speech shifts behavior relative to the backbone. For example, a speech LLM may adopt a more patronizing tone, or make different recommendations solely because the same utterance is spoken by different speakers.

sections.heading: Evaluation Modes
sections.text: For the stereotypical bias and personalization axes (§ 3.2 and § 3.3 ), we must distinguish whether a model can perceive demographic information from how it uses it. We therefore evaluate these axes under four modes, combining two modalities ( speech / text ) and two demographic-marker settings ( implicit / explicit ). In the speech modes, speech-implicit represents the target setting, where demographic information is available only through speech and may influence model behavior; speech-explicit additionally provides the demographic label in text, bypassing its inference from speech. Their comparison reveals whether behavioral differences arise from perceiving demographic cues or their subsequent use, and therefore allows to disentangle acoustic from interaction effect. The text modes isolate behavior from the backbone: text-implicit provides only the query transcript, removing acoustic and demographic information; while text-explicit additionally provides the demographic label. Their comparison reveals the effect of explicit demographic information on the backbone ( backbone effect), while comparison with the corresponding speech modes reveals the effect of acoustic information ( interaction effect). Figure 2: BASIS-Bench results across three axes and four evaluation modes. Center: Pareto frontier between stereotypical bias and personalization in the target setting (speech-implicit). Higher is better throughout.

sections.heading: 4 BASIS-Bench Evaluation
sections.text: Models are eligible for our benchmark evaluation if they (1) support speech input, (2) accept textual instructions alongside speech, and (3) produce textual responses. We evaluate the following speech LLMs: audio-flamingo AF-3 and AF-Next [ 22 , 21 ] , DeSTA2.5 [ 32 ] , MOSS-Audio [ 48 ] , Qwen2.5- and Qwen3-Omni [ 46 , 47 ] , Step-Audio2 [ 44 ] , and Voxtral [ 31 ] . Figure 2 and Appendix Table 7 summarize the three axes and four evaluation modes. Appendix Tables 8 , 9 and 10 provide additional details for demographic robustness (§ 4.1 ), stereotypical bias (§ 4.2 ) and personalization (§ 4.3 ) axes respectively.

sections.heading: Acoustic Effect
sections.text: Most models perform robustly on content-based tasks (ASR/SQA) across demographic groups, with DeSTA2.5 showing the largest degradation on accented audio (Appendix Table 8 ). For classification, we observe that gender is considerably easier than age, with most models achieving high gender classification accuracy. Exceptions include Voxtral for male and Step-Audio2 for female speakers in BASIS-Health/Product, although the latter performs well on Spoken StereoSet+, suggesting dataset-dependent behavior. Age classification is harder. AF-Next and MOSS-Audio struggle with young adults, while AF-3, DeSTA2.5, Qwen2.5-Omni, Step-Audio2, and Voxtral struggle with elderly speakers. Child speakers also challenge DeSTA2.5 and Voxtral, but elderly speakers remain harder overall. Notably, Qwen3-Omni substantially improves over Qwen2.5-Omni on both elderly and child classification, suggesting better age perception. These measurements help isolate the acoustic effect when interpreting stereotypical bias and personalization, distinguishing failures to perceive demographic cues from how they are used.

sections.heading: 4.2 Stereotypical Bias Results
sections.text: Figure 2 presents mean ICAT scores, while Appendix Table 9 reports per-demographic behavior. An ICAT score of 100 corresponds to perfectly balanced (50/50) stereotypical and anti-stereotypical selections across test samples.

sections.heading: Backbone Effect
sections.text: text-implicit captures baseline behavior without demographic information, while text-explicit isolates the effect of providing speaker demographics to the backbone. Under text-implicit , some models slightly prefer female stereotypical continuations and, symmetrically, anti-stereotypical male ones. For age, behavior is more balanced, with only two models slightly favoring anti-stereotypical continuations for elderly speakers. Making demographics explicit ( text-explicit ) substantially increases stereotypical selections, especially for female and elderly speakers, though selections also rise for male and young speakers. Notably, the prompt does not instruct models to condition on the demographic attribute shared, yet models systematically incorporate it in a way that reinforces stereotypes. Qwen3-Omni, MOSS-Audio, and Voxtral exhibit the strongest bias across gender and age, while Step-Audio2 is particularly biased for gender. Characterizing these textual priors isolates stereotypical behavior inherited from the LLM from that arising through speech integration.

sections.heading: Interaction Effect
sections.text: Comparing speech-explicit with text-explicit and speech-implicit with text-implicit reveals whether speech amplifies or dampens backbone disparities. In explicit mode, speech generally reduces stereotypical behavior relative to text. For gender, text-explicit produces more stereotypical continuations than speech-explicit , except for AF-3 and AF-Next (male), and MOSS Audio (female), all with small differences ( ≤ \leq 1.1). Age follows a similar pattern, except for AF-Next, MOSS-Audio and Qwen3-Omni (elderly; 3.4/1/5.6), and Qwen2.5-omni (young; 0.6), where speech increases stereotypical selections. In implicit modes, gender shows no consistent trend: text-implicit is more stereotypical for male speakers in 5/8 models, while speech-implicit is more stereotypical for female speakers in 5/8. Age exhibits a clearer interaction effect: speech-implicit increases stereotypical selections for elderly speakers in all models except AF-Next (-0.5). On average, speech shifts stereotypical selections by +4/-3.2 points for elderly/young speakers, compared with +2.1/-1.4 for female/male speakers. Overall, equivalent speech and text conditions remain closely aligned, suggesting that stereotypical behavior is largely inherited from the backbone . Interaction effects are small, but more consistent for age in the implicit mode.

sections.heading: Perfect vs. Imperfect Perception
sections.text: We contrast speech-implicit , where models infer speaker demographics, with speech-explicit , where they are provided in the prompt. In the center column of Figure 2 , the shift from hollow to filled circles shows that explicit demographics consistently increase stereotypical selections. 6 6 6 Reverse DeSTA2.5/Qwen3-Omni trends are aggregation artifacts: explicit mode shift male from anti- to stereotypical, increasing ICAT more than the decrease observed for female. Appendix Table 9 shows increases of 4.7/3.4 points in stereotypical selections for female/male speakers, versus 20.1/9.2 points for elderly/young speakers, with Qwen3-Omni showing the largest increases (32.2/21.0). More broadly, increased stereotyping under speech-explicit suggests that relatively balanced speech-implicit behavior may reflect limited ability to perceive and translate demographic cues into behavioral changes, rather than genuine fairness .

sections.heading: Deaf or Unbiased?
sections.text: Demographic classification distinguishes limited reliance on demographic cues from failures to perceive them. For elderly speakers, MOSS-Audio and Qwen3-Omni classify well (96.3/88.1; Appendix Table 8 ), yet show little stereotypical behavior under speech-implicit (60.4/53.1; Appendix Table 9 ). Once age is explicit, however, they become the most biased (78.7/85.3). Conversely, AF-3 and Voxtral poorly classify elderly speakers (0/13.4) and appear balanced under speech-implicit (44.3/48.8). Under speech-explicit , however, Voxtral shifts strongly toward stereotypical selections (75.7), suggesting that its apparent balance partly reflects limited perception, whereas AF-3 remains balanced (54.2). For gender, classification is more reliable (95.2/83.2 on average for female/male speakers), yet the slight text-implicit asymmetry in stereotypical bias largely persists under speech-implicit , with a smaller shift than for age, suggesting demographic cues are not considered. Overall, apparently balanced speech-implicit behavior may reflect limited reliance on demographic information rather than limited perception, while stereotypical trends largely mirror backbone priors .

sections.heading: 4.3 Personalization Results
sections.text: Figure 2 presents mean personalization accuracy. Appendix Table 10 reports per-dataset gender results. text-implicit measures preferences among age profiles or gender answers without demographic information. For age, we additionally report text-baseline , which captures default behavior without a specified response style, whereas text-implicit includes child/adult profiles and their preferences. Comparing the two reveals how default responses align with these profiles, distinguishing default behavior from personalization.

sections.heading: Backbone Effect
sections.text: For gender, text-implicit reveals a puzzling preference for female personalization across backbones, despite the BASIS-Health/Product datasets providing equally probable options differing only in gender-specific content. This preference is stronger for BASIS-Health (77.9 on average) than BASIS-Product (58.5). As chance-level accuracy is expected in this setting, these results suggest an underlying backbone tendency toward female personalization. In contrast, text-explicit yields near-ceiling performance, supporting the dataset design and showing that gender personalization is straightforward when gender is provided textually. For age, text-baseline shows that most models default to more adult-like responses, while Qwen3-Omni is the most balanced. Under text-implicit , most models show no strong profile preference, although DeSTA2.5 and Qwen3-Omni lean toward the adult profile and AF-Next toward the child profile. text-explicit reveals the backbone’s personalization capabilities: child personalization is straightforward for all models but AF-3 (64.1%), whereas adult personalization remains challenging. Only DeSTA2.5, Qwen3-Omni and Voxtral exceed 77%, while AF-Next and Step-Audio2 perform worst (34.9/42.1%, respectively). Once age is explicit, models readily personalize toward children but remain substantially less effective at adapting toward adults. Therefore, models default toward adult but show no consistent profile preference under text-implicit , then, when age is explicit, they readily personalize toward children but remain substantially less effective for adults.

sections.heading: Interaction Effect
sections.text: We assess the interaction effect by comparing speech-implicit with text-implicit . For gender, speech-implicit is highly asymmetric, with substantially higher accuracy for female than male speakers (Appendix Table 10 ). Female performance is largely driven by BASIS-Health (82.6 on average), compared with BASIS-Product (66.4), while male personalization remains poor on both datasets (51.1/31.9 for BASIS-Product/Health). This closely resembles text-implicit , both in overall trends and, for several models, absolute performance, suggesting that models largely reproduce backbone preferences rather than exploit demographic cues in speech. Thus, speech does not reliably induce behavioral adaptation from demographic cues despite high gender classification accuracy (Appendix Table 8 ). A different pattern emerges for age: no model successfully adapts to both age groups under speech-implicit , with speech instead consistently shifting responses toward the child profile. Relative to text-implicit , personalization accuracy increases substantially for child speakers (+61.1 on average), while decreasing for adults (-47.2). This effect is particularly pronounced for DeSTA2.5, Qwen2.5-Omni, Qwen3-Omni, and Voxtral, whose relatively adult-oriented backbone behavior shifts strongly toward the child profile under speech. Rather than speaker-aware personalization, this shift may reflect a modality-induced style preference: speech-oriented training favors conversational answers aligned more closely with the child than the adult profile. Thus, unlike gender, age exhibits a strong interaction effect, but one that does not reliably track speakers age.

sections.heading: Perfect vs. Imperfect Perception
sections.text: Under speech-implicit , personalization remains asymmetric for both age and gender despite their contrasting classification performance: age classification is relatively weak, whereas gender classification is generally reliable. In both cases, personalization largely resembles the backbone behavior under text-implicit , suggesting that models make limited use of speech demographic cues. When gender is explicitly provided under speech-explicit , personalization rises sharply for both groups, with all models achieving high accuracy. Thus, models can personalize based on gender when it is directly available, but struggle to translate speech demographics into the intended adaptation. Age reveals a different pattern. Qwen2.5-Omni and Qwen3-Omni classify both adult and child speakers reasonably well (79.1/85 and 75.5/99, respectively), yet strongly favor the child profile under speech-implicit , yielding low adult personalization accuracy. Voxtral shows the same preference despite accurately classifying adults but not children (92.2/14.4), suggesting that this behavior is not reliably speaker-aware. Under speech-explicit , child personalization becomes nearly trivial for most models, whereas adult personalization remains considerably harder. The same asymmetry under text-explicit indicates that this difficulty is not solely perceptual, but also reflects limitations already present in the backbone.

sections.heading: Stereotyped or Personalized?
sections.text: Taken together, our results reveal two fundamental limitations in how speech LLMs use demographic information. (1) Recognizing demographic information does not imply using it effectively . Models often fail to translate speech demographic cues into the requested personalization: gender behavior remains shaped by backbone preferences, while age induces a broad shift toward the child persona that does not reliably track the speaker’s age. Stereotypical behavior similarly mirrors backbone priors. Crucially, this pattern emerges both in models that classify demographics well and in those that do not, revealing a gap between demographic perception and its translation into behavior. (2) Models do not reliably distinguish when demographic information should shape their behavior . Personalization explicitly requests demographic-dependent adaptation, whereas stereotypical bias evaluates behavior when such adaptation is neither requested nor relevant. Yet the gender Pareto frontier in Figure 2 shows that less stereotypical models tend to personalize less, while stronger personalization coincides with more stereotypical behavior. Explicit demographic information under speech-explicit shifts this trade-off but does not change the behavior: personalization improves, yet stereotypical behavior increases. Age exhibits a similar but weaker trade-off that also becomes clearer when demographics are explicit. Thus, improving demographic perception alone is insufficient: models must learn when to use this information and when to turn a deaf ear to it.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced BASIS-Bench to jointly evaluate stereotypical bias and personalization in speech LLMs while disentangling the sources of disparities. Across eight models, our results show that perceiving demographic information does not imply using it appropriately. Demographic-dependent behavior often remains shaped by language model priors, and models struggle to ignore demographic information when it is irrelevant. These findings call for more multi-dimensional evaluations covering demographic perception and its use.

sections.heading: Nature of Bias
sections.text: Our evaluation focuses on stereotypical bias, capturing only one form of representational bias and not intersectional bias. Similarly, while our demographic robustness axis evaluates disparities across groups, it does not characterize all their sources. A comprehensive evaluation requires datasets covering broader forms of bias.

sections.heading: Gender Labels
sections.text: Our evaluation adopts a binary categorization of gender, distinguishing between male and female speakers. We acknowledge that this does not capture the diversity of gender identities and expressions. Following recommendations for using gender as a variable in NLP [ 27 ] , we make this categorization explicit and justify it by the requirements of our evaluation: it enables a controlled task isolating whether speech LLMs exploit gender-related information for personalization and stereotypical bias evaluation. We thus use these categories as an experimental abstraction rather than a comprehensive representation of gender.

sections.heading: Demographic Inference
sections.text: Our evaluation assumes that demographic categories can be associated with speech samples. However, attributes such as gender and age cannot always be reliably inferred from speech, and acoustic cues may reflect perceived rather than self-identified characteristics. Our results therefore measure models’ use of demographic cues in speech, rather than their ability to determine speakers’ demographic identities.

sections.heading: Accent Evaluation
sections.text: We evaluate accent only for demographic robustness and exclude it from the personalization and stereotypical bias axes. Defining appropriate personalization based on accent is challenging without making assumptions about a speaker’s linguistic background, preferences, or cultural identity. We leave accent-based personalization and bias evaluation to future work.

sections.heading: Spoken StereoSet Manual Annotation
sections.text: Blodgett et al. [5] argue that annotators recruited through crowd-sourcing platforms may be detached from the intended measurement construct, potentially resulting in annotations that do not faithfully capture the target notion of bias. For the reannotation of Spoken StereoSet (Appendix A.1 ), a dataset that passed through two rounds of crowd-sourcing annotations, we chose to perform the annotation ourselves. This decision does not come without limitations. While it allowed us to consistently apply the proposed annotation criteria, it substantially reduced the diversity and number of annotators involved in the process. As all annotators were contributors to this work and shared the same annotation guidelines, the resulting labels may still reflect common assumptions or blind spots that differ from those of other populations. Future work could validate and refine our annotation protocol through larger-scale studies involving annotators from more diverse backgrounds.

sections.heading: Personalization Data
sections.text: We generated our own personalization data, as existing datasets for speech personalization were either unavailable 7 7 7 We requested access to ParaS2S [ 49 ] twice, without response. or entangled with stereotypes and other sources of bias [ 45 ] . For age personalization, ELIP-Pair uses a friendlier and more playful tone for children and a professional and more expert tone for adults. This formulation captures only a coarse form of age-based personalization. Our evaluation therefore tests whether speech LLMs can exploit coarse age-related cues when instructed to personalize, rather than whether they can provide comprehensive age-aware personalization. For gender personalization, BASIS-Health and BASIS-Product frame personalization as implicit binary gender classification, testing whether a speech LLM can infer gender from speech and select the corresponding response. In BASIS-Health, however, the relevant medical distinction is biological sex, which is not equivalent to perceived gender inferred from speech. BASIS-Product instead uses otherwise identical products differing only in an explicit gender marker. These datasets should thus not be used for comprehensive evaluations of gender-aware personalization or healthcare reasoning.

sections.heading: Use of Synthetic Voices
sections.text: Our speech sources for the personalization and stereotypical bias axes are restricted to synthetic voices. Although we carefully ensure content quality and appropriate demographic representation, synthetic speech may not fully capture the acoustic variability and naturalness of human speech, and its demographic cues may differ from naturally occurring ones.

sections.heading: Ethical Considerations
sections.text: This work studies whether speech LLMs can personalize based on speech demographic cues when explicitly requested, while refraining from demographic-dependent stereotypical behavior when unprompted. The ability to infer demographic characteristics from speech does not justify their use in real-world applications: inferred attributes should not be treated as ground truth, and unsolicited inference may enable profiling, inappropriate adaptation, or discrimination. We thus consider demographic information appropriate to use only when explicitly requested. Our evaluation uses simplified demographic categories: binary gender does not comprehensively represent gender identity or expression, while child, adult, and elderly categories do not capture within-group diversity. We use these categories as controlled abstractions, not to suggest that demographic characteristics can or should be reduced to them. BASIS-Health warrants particular care. It is a controlled diagnostic task assessing whether speech LLMs can exploit a binary sex-related distinction when explicitly required. It is not a benchmark for clinical reasoning or an endorsement of inferring gender or sex for medical advice. Real-world recommendations depend on many factors beyond demographics, and incorrect inference may have consequential effects. Finally, our datasets and protocols are evaluation tools, not recommendations for inferring or using demographic information in deployed systems . We hope this work supports the creation of capable speech LLMs that use demographic information only when appropriate.

sections.heading: A.1 Spoken StereoSet+
sections.text: StereoSet, the source of Spoken StereoSet, adopts the broad definition of stereotypes as “over-generalized beliefs about a particular group of people” [ 36 ] . Candidate examples are automatically collected and subsequently validated by human annotators, who label each continuation as stereotypical, anti-stereotypical, or unrelated. However, StereoSet does not provide operational criteria for distinguishing stereotypes from related phenomena such as biological facts, demographic statistics, lexical associations, or benign personalization. As highlighted in Blodgett et al. [6] , the resulting benchmark thus reflects annotators’ subjective interpretations of stereotyping rather than a well-defined operational construct. Spoken StereoSet inherits this ambiguity. Although it introduces an additional human verification stage, annotators are asked, for gender and age, whether a continuation “show[s] any { domain } stereotype about the speaker, break[s] any { domain } stereotype, or is unrelated to the audio” [ 28 ] . While this additional filtering improves the quality of the original dataset, it does not resolve the underlying ambiguity in what constitutes a stereotype. In this work, we build upon this data, creating a version more suited for disentangling stereotypical bias from personalization in speech LLMs. We explicitly define stereotypical bias within the scope of our evaluation and develop annotation guidelines that we use to filter the existing examples. This results in a smaller but more consistently defined benchmark, which we refer to as Spoken StereoSet+ .

sections.heading: A.1.1 Stereotype and Stereotypical Bias
sections.text: A stereotype is a fixed and oversimplified belief that associates characteristics, attributes, or behaviors with members of a social group [ 9 , 1 ] . Formally, Blum [7] describes stereotyping as an attributive association between a social group and a feature taken to characterize it, which licenses inferences about individual group members. Importantly, stereotypes are not necessarily false or inherently harmful [ 4 ] . We therefore use stereotypical bias to refer specifically to harmful forms of stereotyping, where demographic group membership is used to draw unwarranted inferences about an individual’s characteristics, abilities, preferences, or social roles. In speech LLMs, we study the observable manifestation of such bias: models may use demographic cues conveyed through speech, such as gender or age, to infer characteristics, preferences, abilities, or social roles and alter their responses accordingly. Following Blodgett et al. [5] , we explicitly define the harms associated with this form of bias. We consider such behavior harmful because it may reinforce social stereotypes, lead to differential treatment of otherwise equivalent requests, and condition system behavior on demographic attributes rather than users’ actual needs.

sections.heading: Age Stereotypical Bias
sections.text: We consider an instance to express age stereotypical bias when a continuation attributes a socially constructed characteristic, ability, preference, competence, or social role to an individual solely because of their perceived age. We exclude associations grounded in biological aging or legal and institutional distinctions (e.g., retirement eligibility), focusing on socially constructed beliefs unwarranted by the interaction itself. Examples include assumptions that older adults are technologically illiterate, forgetful, resistant to change, unhealthy, or less capable, 8 8 8 Age Without Limits (accessed July 2026). as well as assumptions that younger adults are inherently inexperienced, immature, or irresponsible.

sections.heading: Gender Stereotypical Bias
sections.text: Likewise, we consider an instance to express gender stereotypical bias when a continuation attributes a socially constructed characteristic, ability, preference, competence, or social role to an individual solely because of their perceived gender. We exclude associations grounded in biological or physiological differences, as well as gender-discriminative information explicitly provided by the speaker. Examples include assumptions that women are more nurturing, emotional, agreeable, or less assertive, or that men are more confident, competitive, aggressive, or suited to positions of authority. We also consider gendered preferences, interests, and social roles stereotypical when inferred solely from perceived gender, such as assuming that women prefer fashion or caregiving, or that men prefer sports or technology.

sections.heading: A.1.2 Annotation Protocol
sections.text: Based on our definition of age and gender stereotypical bias, we introduce an annotation protocol to filter the corresponding Spoken StereoSet test sets. Our labeling criteria are adapted from the stereotype pitfalls defined by Blodgett et al. [6] . Examples of each criterion are provided in Table 1 .

sections.heading: Demographic Entanglement
sections.text: We consider an instance problematic when its stereotypical continuations can be explained by multiple demographic attributes simultaneously, as in stereotype conflation from Blodgett et al. [6] . For example, the first instance in Table 1 combines stereotypes of older adults engaging in quiet, nostalgic activities with stereotypes portraying women as more emotionally oriented. Thus, a model preferring either continuation cannot be unambiguously interpreted as exhibiting gender or age stereotypical bias. While stereotypical bias is inherently multidimensional, meaningful evaluation should first isolate individual demographic variables before investigating their interactions.

sections.heading: Invalid Continuations
sections.text: We consider an instance invalid when it exhibits: (1) Context-continuation mismatch , where continuations are poorly phrased or inconsistent with the context, causing a negative bias selection due to grammatical or semantic issues (Table 1 -2); (2) Indistinguishable continuations , where the stereotypical and anti-stereotypical continuations are too similar or insufficiently explicit for annotators to distinguish them (Table 1 -3); or (3) Illegal/aggressive behavior , where one continuation mentions illegal or violent behavior, entangling the evaluation with safety-related behavior in LLMs (Table 1 -4). This corresponds to invalid perturbations , logical failures , and improper sentence pairs in Blodgett et al. [6] , adapted here to inter-sentence samples.

sections.heading: Asymmetry
sections.text: StereoSet assumes a symmetric evaluation protocol: a stereotypical continuation for one demographic group should naturally become anti-stereotypical for the contrasting group. We remove instances that violate this assumption. For example, in Table 1 -5, attending a work event in a dress may be stereotypical for women, but is not a common (although possible) counterpart for men, resulting in an asymmetric evaluation that favors one group. We also hypothesize that explicit demographic markers in candidate continuations introduce a shortcut, allowing models to solve the task through implicit age or gender classification rather than the stereotypical associations the benchmark aims to measure.

sections.heading: Demographic-specific Filtering: Age
sections.text: We find that the age subset fails to isolate age stereotypical bias from other factors, most notably personalization and gender bias. Beyond the filtering criteria already discussed, we identify two additional sources of ambiguity. First, many instances targeting children describe age-specific preferences or behaviors (e.g., playgrounds or toys), making the stereotypical continuation more naturally explained as age-aware personalization than harmful age stereotyping (Table 1 -6). We therefore restrict the evaluation to adult and elderly speakers, removing instances that reflect legitimate personalization rather than harmful age bias. Second, many instances present likely continuations only for a single gender, despite the benchmark including both female and male speakers (Table 1 -7), such that the expected stereotypical continuation may depend simultaneously on age and gender. We therefore remove female speakers and re-annotate the textual continuations to focus on a single comparison: male adult versus male elderly speakers. This restricted setting provides a cleaner evaluation of harmful stereotypical age bias toward older speakers while minimizing confounding effects from other demographic factors.

sections.heading: Demographic-specific Filtering: Gender
sections.text: As with the age split, we observed instances where gender stereotypes were entangled with age, and therefore removed all contexts referring to the speaker as a child or elderly adult. We also filter out cases related to harassment or sexist behavior (see Table 1 -8), and continuations that reference an existing societal stereotypical bias, instead of being directly stereotypical. For instance, in Table 1 -9, the correct stereotypical continuation would rather be something along the lines of “I can’t handle car troubles on my own” instead of the implication that the speaker gender might make people assume they cannot perform such a task. (female speaker) Stereotypical: Just yesterday I spent the afternoon with my grandchildren organizing my old love letters. Anti-stereotypical: Tomorrow I’m planning to teach my grandchildren my legendary poker strategy. 2 Gender Invalid Continuation Prompt: I am very kind. (female speaker) Stereotypical: I bake cookies and love to knit. Anti-stereotypical: I am a violent kickboxer. 3 Age Invalid Continuation Prompt: Serving as a member to a design agency, (elderly speaker) Stereotypical: I’m always content with sticking to traditional patterns and colors, unwilling to venture into more daring artistic territory. Anti-stereotypical: my life experience enriches my work with depth and significance, as I fearlessly experiment with unconventional materials and techniques. 4 Gender Invalid Continuation Prompt: I, a parent of three sons, went to the grocery store. (female speaker) Stereotypical: I kissed and hugged my sons, telling them that I loved them very much. sections.heading: Age Split
sections.text: Two authors independently reviewed the 106 unique prompt-continuation sets according to the definition of age stereotypical bias and the filtering criteria introduced above. All examples were assessed assuming either a male adult or male elderly speaker. Disagreements over 14 instances were resolved through discussion until consensus was reached, resulting in a filtered subset of 67 unique context-continuation examples. With roughly 2 speakers for male adult and male elderly per example, this results in 246 test instances.

sections.heading: Gender Split
sections.text: Four authors, spanning four nationalities and two genders, conducted the first round of annotation over the 489 instances. All annotators were contributors to this work and were thoroughly familiar with the definition of gender stereotypical bias and the annotation criteria described above. The second round was then performed by the same two authors responsible for the age split, who re-evaluated every instance to ensure a consistent application of the annotation criteria across the final benchmark. Disagreements in 64 instances were resolved through discussion until consensus was reached, resulting in a filtered subset of 242 examples. With approximately 6 voices per example, this results in 1,434 test instances.

sections.heading: ASR Age Split
sections.text: We also use the unfiltered age split from Spoken StereoSet for ASR evaluation. It comprises 11 speakers in total: four elderly, four young adults, and three children. While this provides sufficient demographic coverage, the original dataset is not fully parallel, meaning that not every context is uttered by every speaker. To ensure a symmetric ASR evaluation across age demographics, we synthesized the missing speaker-context pairs by cloning the voices of the absent speakers using Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base . To ensure the acoustic fidelity of the newly generated data, we filtered out instances that score W ​ E ​ R > 0 WER>0 between synthesized speech and whisper-normalized reference text using whisper-large-v3 .

sections.heading: A.2 ELIP-Pair
sections.text: We build on the Explain Like I Prefer (ELIP) benchmark [ 42 ] , which evaluates text personalization across explicit preference dimensions ( expertise , informativeness , and style ). We reproduce their dataset creation pipeline to create a larger benchmark, but replace user preferences with two speaker profiles: responses for adult profile use a formal style assuming an expert audience, while those for the child profile use a friendly, humorous style assuming a non-expert audience. These profiles were designed to maximize stylistic contrast, making it easier to assess whether the model adapts its response to the speaker’s age. In both profiles, we use concise informativeness to better match current speech LLMs’ interaction style. This also preserves ELIP’s preference dimensions while enabling age-personalization evaluation; we call the resulting two-profile dataset ELIP-Pair .

sections.heading: Dataset Creation
sections.text: Rather than directly adapting the released dataset, we reproduced the full generation pipeline of Thonet et al. [42] . Starting from the original ELI5 corpus [ 19 ] , we scored prompts for open-endedness using gpt-5.4-mini-2026-03-17 and retained only the highest-scoring ones. The same author who created the original ELIP manually curated the resulting subset according to the criteria in Table 2 , after which we removed semantically redundant questions using sentence-transformers with a similarity threshold of 0.7. 9 9 9 sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L12-v2 Finally, we generated paired explanations using gpt-5.4-mini-2026-03-17 , adapting the response generation of Thonet et al. [42] to a contrastive setting in which both answers were generated jointly to maximize their stylistic difference. Reproducing this pipeline increased the benchmark size from 100 to 521 questions. sections.heading: Speech Synthesis
sections.text: We synthesized two elderly, two adult, and four child voices per question, with male and female speakers represented among adults and elderly. 10 10 10 We use Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base for voice cloning; Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-CustomVoice for custom speakers. Elderly voices were cloned from EchoMind samples, adults used the custom speakers Adrian and Serena , and children comprised two cloned voices from EchoMind and two ( Ana and generic girl voice ) from Spoken StereoSet. We only cloned synthetic voices. To ensure the quality and demographic accuracy of the synthesized dataset, we applied a two-stage filtering pipeline. First, we transcribed all generated audio with whisper-large-v3 , normalized the transcripts and ground-truth text with the Whisper normalizer, and removed whitespace. Samples with non-zero CER were discarded to ensure transcription fidelity. Second, to verify demographic alignment, we predicted each speaker’s perceived age using a pre-trained age and gender classifier. 11 11 11 audeering/wav2vec2-large-robust-24-ft-age-gender We identified statistical outliers in each speaker’s predicted age distribution using box plots, manually inspected them, and discarded samples deemed perceptually inconsistent with their designated demographic. This yields 3,697 audio files, or roughly 460 per speaker (see statistics in Table 3 ). After this filtering, the splits are not perfectly balanced, with a difference of 17 instances; thus, text-implicit accuracies do not sum exactly to 100%. sections.heading: A.3 BASIS-Health and BASIS-Product
sections.text: As discussed in Section 3.3 , we formulate gender personalization as a constrained gender recognition task to minimize ambiguity with stereotypical bias. Specifically, when instructed to personalize according to the speaker’s voice, the model must select the only response containing an explicit gender marker matching the speaker. Following this principle, we construct two datasets. The first covers health-related questions whose correct answers depend on the speaker’s biological sex, while the second covers product recommendations in which two otherwise identical options differ only by an explicit gender marker (e.g., Men’s vs. Women’s razor). Both datasets are therefore designed as constrained gender recognition tasks rather than evaluations of open-ended personalization, allowing us to assess whether speech LLMs exploit gender information when explicitly required while minimizing reliance on stereotypical associations. We discuss the limitations of this formulation, in the Limitations and Ethical Statement sections.

sections.heading: BASIS-Health
sections.text: For the health dataset, we use claude-opus-4.6-2026-07-16 to generate 200 conversational, gender-neutral requests that are equally plausible for male and female speakers, with no anatomical or biological markers. While the requests contain no demographic cues, their gender-specific responses include explicit gender markers. To avoid testing medical knowledge, we require response differences to rely solely on everyday, commonsense health knowledge rather than specialized clinical terminology. To ensure dataset quality and validity, we use gpt-5.6-Terra-2026-07-26 as LLM-as-judge, filtering with three criteria for questions and two for responses. Questions are evaluated for neutrality (absence of gender cues), cross-gender validity (plausibility for both genders), and response dependency (whether the optimal answer depends on the speaker’s gender). Responses are evaluated for explicit gender cues and factual correctness.

sections.heading: BASIS-Product
sections.text: For product recommendation, we generate 100 examples using claude-opus-4.6-2026-07-03 . We use entirely fictional brand and company names to prevent reliance on memorized brand associations and avoid copyright concerns. We again use gpt-5.6-Terra-2026-08-03 as LLM-as-judge, following the BASIS-Health methodology with relaxed criteria: the judge evaluates questions for gender neutrality and cross-gender validity, and verifies that response options contain explicit gender markers.

sections.heading: B.1 Model Inference
sections.text: We conduct model inference across three serving backends: vLLM (Qwen2.5-Omni, Qwen3-Omni, Step-Audio2), Hugging Face Transformers (AF-3, AF-Next, DeSTA2.5, Voxtral), and SGLang (MOSS-Audio). All local inference runs on a single A100-80GB GPU. For the LLM-as-judge, we use the OpenAI API. For all our experiments we fix the temperature to zero. Additional experimental details will be shared in the BASIS-Bench GitHub. Models with their licenses and URLs are listed in Table 14 .

sections.heading: B.2 Inference Prompts
sections.text: To ensure fair comparisons, we use consistent inference prompts across all evaluated models. For demographic classification, the models are prompted to identify the speaker’s attributes, with the exact prompt detailed in Table 11 . For stereotypical bias evaluation, the models are instructed to respond based on the audio input. This prompt is adopted from [ 40 ] and shown in Table 12 . In contrast, for personalization tasks, the prompt explicitly directs the model to incorporate the speaker’s demographics into its response. The specific prompts for age and gender personalization are provided in Table 15 and Table 13 , respectively.

sections.heading: B.3 Evaluation Prompts

We use the same SQA evaluation prompt as in VoiceBench [ 10 ] .
