Kshitij Ambilduke 1,2 Caroline Brun 2 Thibaut Thonet 2 Vassilina Nikoulina 2 Marcely Zanon Boito 2 Corresponding author: marcely.zanon-boito@naverlabs.com Abstract Recent speech LLMs can leverage rich paralinguistic cues, enabling more complex and personalized interactions. However, little work investigates how this sensitivity can lead to stereotyping, and existing evaluations largely measure demographic disparities without distinguishing beneficial personalization from stereotypical behavior. We introduce BASIS-Bench , a benchmark designed to disentangle these two aspects through three axes: (1) demographic robustness , measuring disparities in content-based tasks across speakers and demographic classification capabilities; (2) stereotypical bias , measuring whether perceived demographic cues trigger unprompted stereotypical behavior; and (3) personalization , measuring whether models can tailor responses to demographic characteristics when explicitly requested. We evaluate eight recent speech LLMs and find that, despite often recognizing demographic cues, most fail to translate them into appropriate personalization. Explicit demographic labels improve personalization but also amplify stereotypical associations already present in the textual backbones. These findings highlight the need to train speech LLMs not only to perceive demographic cues, but to learn when they should shape their responses. 1 Introduction Speech LLMs are increasingly capable of leveraging not only linguistic content but also information conveyed by the speaker’s voice, enabling more natural and personalized interactions. In particular, speech provides demographic cues such as age and gender that are unavailable from linguistic content alone. This creates a new challenge: a capable speech assistant should exploit these cues when appropriate, while ignoring them when they are irrelevant or could lead to unfair, stereotypical, or otherwise inappropriate behavior. Personalization and stereotypical bias are therefore not independent phenomena, but two outcomes of the same underlying sensitivity to speaker characteristics, distinguished by whether demographic cues are used when relevant or irrelevant to the task. Yet, existing speech LLMs evaluations do not always cleanly disentangle these aspects. Bias benchmarks typically assess demographic disparities under controlled linguistic content, encompassing stereotypical bias towards demographic groups [ 28 ] as well as performance and recommendation disparities [ 45 ] . Meanwhile, some personalization and paralinguistic-aware benchmarks reward demographic-dependent changes in model responses even when such adaptation is not explicitly requested by the user [ 2 , 49 ] . 1 1 1 For instance, ParaS2S rewards gender-tailored responses without an explicit request for personalization; SD-Eval rewards mimicking the speaker’s accent without such a request. Thus, similar demographic-dependent behavior may be rewarded as personalization or penalized as stereotyping across evaluations. Motivated by Kantharuban et al. [26] , we distinguish these outcomes by considering demographic personalization desirable only when explicitly requested. Building on this distinction, we introduce BASIS-Bench ( B ias A nd per S onalization I n S peech LLMs Bench mark). We define three evaluation axes: (1) demographic robustness , measuring disparities in content-related tasks across speakers and demographic classification capabilities; (2) stereotypical bias , measuring whether perceived demographic cues trigger stereotypical behavior when they are irrelevant to the task; and (3) personalization , measuring whether models can tailor responses to demographic characteristics when explicitly requested. To characterize the sources of demographic-dependent behavior along these axes, we further distinguish three potential effects: the acoustic effect , arising from speech encoding; the backbone effect , inherited from the underlying language model; and the interaction effect , arising from their interaction. Together, this framework allows us to isolate different sources of demographic disparity and distinguish failures to process speech and perceive demographic information from its appropriate or inappropriate use. Our results show that recent speech LLMs achieve similar content-based task performance across demographic groups and often correctly identify speakers’ demographic characteristics. Yet, consistent with previous work [ 49 ] , most models show limited personalization across age and gender when demographic information must be inferred from speech. Providing them explicitly via text substantially improves personalization, suggesting that these failures primarily reflect difficulty translating speech demographic cues into appropriate behavior changes rather than an inability to personalize. Conversely, models consistently exhibit stereotypical behavior toward female and elderly speakers. This behavior is amplified by explicit demographic information but persists when speech is replaced by its transcription, suggesting that much of it originates in the backbone rather than from the use of speech. Together, these findings suggest that speech LLMs are not yet reliable at deciding when and how demographic information should shape their behavior: they struggle to turn perceived demographic cues into appropriate personalization, yet readily reproduce stereotypes when such information is irrelevant. Our contributions are the following: (1) We introduce BASIS-Bench to disentangle stereotypical bias from personalization while diagnosing three potential sources of demographic-dependent behavior: acoustic, backbone, and interaction effects. (2) We release data resources, including Spoken StereoSet+ , a manually filtered version of the original dataset [ 28 ] with explicit definitions of stereotypical bias and associated harms; ELIP-Pair , an age personalization dataset based on ELIP [ 42 ] ; and BASIS-Health and BASIS-Product , synthetic gender personalization datasets. (3) We provide a comprehensive evaluation of eight popular speech LLMs across demographic robustness, stereotypical bias, and personalization, revealing systematic gaps in how models perceive and use demographic information. 2 Related Work Speech LLMs Following the success of text-only LLMs, numerous speech-native assistants have been proposed for end-to-end spoken interaction, progressively expanding from modeling linguistic content, to jointly modeling acoustic and paralinguistic information such as speaker identity, prosody, emotion, and speaking style [ 39 , 14 , 25 , 46 , 47 , 44 , 15 , 31 , 48 , 32 , 21 , 22 ] . This evolution reflects the growing recognition that effective spoken language interaction requires modeling both linguistic content and acoustic characteristics. Bias in Speech Systems Bias evaluation in speech systems has been extensively studied in recent years [ 13 , 20 , 18 , 8 , 12 , 33 , 34 , 30 , 43 , 3 , 16 , 24 , 23 ] . We highlight that while speech LLMs are subject to the same sources of demographic disparity as single-purpose systems (e.g., transcription and translation systems), their broader capabilities introduce additional ways in which demographics can affect model behavior. Assessing disparities arising from speech encoding alone is therefore insufficient to capture their potential harms. Data for Speech LLM Bias Evaluation The majority of existing bias datasets for speech LLMs are repurposed from existing textual datasets [ 28 , 29 , 11 ] . Consequently, most evaluate bias primarily through lexical content rather than on acoustic features and their interaction. For example, Choi et al. [11] resynthesize contexts from the text-based BBQ dataset [ 37 ] , thus stereotypical associations are primarily encoded in lexical rather than acoustic cues. We argue that this approach fails to capture the modality-specific biases embedded in end-to-end speech LLMs. A more compelling evaluation protocol must investigate how model behavior shifts in response to demographic information conveyed through speech. Datasets where semantic content remains fixed, but the speaker’s acoustic attributes vary thus provide a more realistic measure of bias in speech LLMs [ 28 , 45 ] . Personalization Recent speech LLM benchmarks such as SD-Eval [ 2 ] , ParaS2S [ 49 ] , and EchoMind [ 51 ] evaluate whether speech LLMs can leverage paralinguistic cues for generating speaker-aware responses, covering cues such as emotion, accent, age, gender, sarcasm, and environmental sounds. SD-Eval and EchoMind take broader approaches spanning multiple paralinguistic and reasoning capabilities, while ParaS2S focuses on speaker traits through incongruent speech scenarios where linguistic content alone cannot determine the appropriate response. Overall, these works show that current models have substantial room for improvement in leveraging paralinguistic cues. In parallel, recent work in the textual domain has investigated to what extent LLMs can derive implicit demographic cues from the user interaction and provide unprompted personalization. Kantharuban et al. [26] show that LLM recommendations can be influenced by explicit or implicit racial identity, producing stereotypical recommendations even when personalization is not requested, while Entezami and Endres [17] find that demographic attributes unrelated to the task can influence AI-assisted software development outputs. In this work, we focus on speech LLMs, jointly evaluating their ability to reliably perceive demographic cues, personalize based on them when requested, and avoid unprompted stereotypical behavior. 3 BASIS-Bench We introduce BASIS-Bench ( B ias A nd per S onalization I n S peech LLMs Bench mark), a benchmark designed to disentangle personalization from stereotypical bias in speech LLMs and diagnose the factors underlying demographic-dependent disparities. Focusing primarily on age and gender, we first introduce three complementary evaluation axes (§ 3.1 - 3.3 ), then define a framework that disentangles the sources of demographic disparity along them (§ 3.4 ). Figure 1 provides an overview, and Appendix B describes additional inference and evaluation settings. Figure 1: Overview of BASIS-Bench : evaluation axes, tasks, demographic dimensions, and datasets. 3.1 Demographic Robustness Axis We use demographic robustness to assess whether speech LLMs can reliably process and perceive speech across speakers with diverse demographic characteristics. We evaluate two complementary capabilities: whether models can perceive demographic cues through age and gender classification, and whether they exhibit performance disparities across speakers on content-based tasks, namely automatic speech recognition (ASR) and spoken question answering (SQA). Together, these evaluations provide context for interpreting the subsequent stereotypical bias and personalization axes by establishing whether models can reliably process speech and perceive demographic cues. Data For ASR, we use Fair-Speech [ 43 ] , Spoken StereoSet+ (ASR Age Split), and SD-QA [ 18 ] . 2 2 2 While our demographic dimensions are age and gender, we additionally consider accent for ASR/SQA to broaden our robustness assessment across diverse speakers. Fair-Speech covers different genders and accents; we do not use its age labels, which span 18-65 years and therefore do not cover children or elderly speakers. We use the Spoken StereoSet+ ASR Age Split (Appendix A.1.3 ) to assess performance across age groups; we describe its construction in § 3.2 . SD-QA covers different accents and it is also used for SQA, while LibriSQA [ 50 ] assesses SQA performance across gender categories. For demographic classification, we use the same data as the other axes, enabling direct comparisons across axes. Evaluation For ASR, we report word error rate (WER) between the gold and generated transcripts after applying the Whisper normalizer [ 38 ] . We cap WER at 100 and report accuracy ( 100 − WER 100-\mathrm{WER} ) averaged for each demographic (accent, gender, and age) and dataset (SD-QA, Fair-Speech, Spoken StereoSet+). For SQA we use LLM-as-judge evaluation, computing mean accuracy for each demographic category (accent and gender) and dataset (SD-QA and LibriSQA) before aggregating across them. We then average the resulting ASR and SQA scores to obtain the context-based score for each model. For demographic classification, we explicitly provide the possible categories in the evaluation prompt, reducing the task to implicit MCQA, and reporting exact-match accuracy per-label. We then average across labels, obtaining the final classification score. 3.2 Stereotypical Bias Axis We use stereotypical bias to refer to harmful forms of stereotyping, where a demographic group is associated with particular characteristics, attributes, or behaviors, and these associations are used to draw unwarranted inferences about individual members [ 7 , 4 ] . In speech LLMs, this can manifest when speech demographic cues, such as gender or age, influence a model’s response based on stereotypical assumptions about a speaker’s characteristics, preferences, abilities, or social roles. Such behavior can reinforce social stereotypes and lead to differential treatment across speakers with equivalent requests. This axis thus assesses whether models exhibit stereotypical behavior based on perceived demographic cues when their use is not explicitly requested. 3 3 3 We provide a discussion of stereotyping, its relationship to bias, and the harms considered in this work in Appendix A.1.1 . Data We build on Spoken StereoSet [ 28 ] , introducing a manual filtering stage to align the dataset with our definition of stereotypical bias for age and gender. We consider adult and elderly male speakers for age, and female and male speakers for gender. We detail our definitions and post-processing in Appendix A.1 , and refer to the resulting dataset as Spoken StereoSet+ . Evaluation We follow the context association test (CAT) from StereoSet [ 36 ] , reporting the proportions of stereotypical and anti-stereotypical continuations. Since irrelevant continuations are negligible, 4 4 4 All models select irrelevant examples in < 2 % <2\% of cases, except DeSTA2.5 for which this rate goes up to 11%. we omit them for brevity. To mitigate positional bias in the MCQA setting [ 40 ] , we evaluate all answer-option permutations and report mean accuracy for both stereotypical and anti-stereotypical continuations. We additionally adopt the idealized CAT (ICAT) score from StereoSet, which jointly captures continuation relevance and the skew between stereotypical and anti-stereotypical choices. ICAT ranges from 0 (maximally biased) to 100 (unbiased). We report the per-demographic mean ICAT score as a single number measuring bias per model, rather than an overall ICAT, to prevent opposing stereotypical and anti-stereotypical behaviors across demographics from balancing out and producing an apparent unbiased score. 3.3 Personalization Axis This axis assesses whether models can use demographic information conveyed through a speaker’s voice to tailor their responses. A key challenge is determining when such adaptation is appropriate, as inferring preferences from age or gender can itself constitute stereotyping. Motivated by Kantharuban et al. [26] , we thus consider personalization appropriate only when explicitly requested. For age personalization , we focus on developmental differences between children and adults, adapting the complexity, style, or presentation of information based on cognitive development differences rather than socially constructed stereotypes. We do not treat elderly speakers as a separate personalization category, as defining age-based adaptations for this group would require assumptions about their cognitive abilities or needs that may themselves be stereotypical. Instead, the adult category spans young to elderly adult speakers. During inference, the model receives a spoken question along with textual descriptions of the adult and child profiles and is asked to answer in the same style as the speaker’s demographic profile. For gender personalization , we similarly find that existing formulations are difficult to disentangle from stereotypical bias. We thus formulate it as a constrained gender recognition task: when explicitly instructed to personalize based on the speaker’s voice, the model must select the only response containing the speaker’s gender marker. We introduce two datasets: BASIS-Health , covering health questions whose answers depend on biological sex, 5 5 5 See Limitations regarding our sex/gender labels. and BASIS-Product , covering product recommendations where identical options differ by the gender marker (e.g., Men’s vs. Women’s razor). These datasets assess whether models exploit gender information when explicitly requested , while minimizing reliance on stereotypical associations. Data For age personalization, we follow Thonet et al. [42] and create and manually validate an expanded version of ELIP, ELIP-Pair , containing 521 questions, each associated with two responses tailored to distinct personas: child and adult. We synthesize child and adult speech by cloning other synthetic voices, and then automatically filtering the result based on both ASR quality and age classification. Outliers are then manually verified. For gender personalization, we create BASIS-Health and BASIS-Product using Claude-Opus, followed by GPT-5.6 filtering, speech synthesis, and similar automatic and manual post-processing from ELIP-Pair. Detailed generation pipelines for these datasets are provided in Appendix A.2 and § A.3 . Evaluation For gender personalization, we report per-demographic accuracy and, as for stereotypical bias, we evaluate all answer-option permutations to mitigate positional bias. For age personalization, we classify the response as child- or adult-oriented using LLM-as-judge. 3.4 Disparity Sources and Evaluation Modes Although bias in speech systems is well studied [ 30 , 43 ] and textual LLMs have been extensively evaluated for demographic bias [ 36 , 37 ] , existing evaluations of speech LLMs lack a systematic framework for distinguishing whether demographic-dependent behavior originates from the speech encoder, the backbone, or their interaction. We therefore distinguish three sources of demographic disparity, and design our evaluation framework to disentangle their contributions. The acoustic effect originates from disparities in the speech encoding process, where speaker characteristics may affect how reliably linguistic content or demographic cues are represented and perceived. For example, strongly accented or non-standard dialectal speech may be less reliably processed than speech varieties overrepresented in training data, resulting in performance gaps. The backbone effect refers to biases and personalization capabilities inherited from the language model, independently of the speech modality. Recent work has shown that LLMs can infer demographic characteristics from implicit cues and exhibit demographic stereotypes and disparate treatment across sensitive attributes [ 36 , 35 , 41 , 26 ] . A speech LLM may therefore inherit tendencies such as occupational gender stereotypes or culturally skewed recommendations, from its backbone. The interaction effect arises from the interaction between speech representations and the backbone. Even when speech is faithfully encoded, demographic and other paralinguistic cues may introduce demographic-dependent behavior or amplify or attenuate biases already present in the backbone. This effect captures how speech shifts behavior relative to the backbone. For example, a speech LLM may adopt a more patronizing tone, or make different recommendations solely because the same utterance is spoken by different speakers. Evaluation Modes For the stereotypical bias and personalization axes (§ 3.2 and § 3.3 ), we must distinguish whether a model can perceive demographic information from how it uses it. We therefore evaluate these axes under four modes, combining two modalities ( speech / text ) and two demographic-marker settings ( implicit / explicit ). In the speech modes, speech-implicit represents the target setting, where demographic information is available only through speech and may influence model behavior; speech-explicit additionally provides the demographic label in text, bypassing its inference from speech. Their comparison reveals whether behavioral differences arise from perceiving demographic cues or their subsequent use, and therefore allows to disentangle acoustic from interaction effect. The text modes isolate behavior from the backbone: text-implicit provides only the query transcript, removing acoustic and demographic information; while text-explicit additionally provides the demographic label. Their comparison reveals the effect of explicit demographic information on the backbone ( backbone effect), while comparison with the corresponding speech modes reveals the effect of acoustic information ( interaction effect). Figure 2: BASIS-Bench results across three axes and four evaluation modes. Center: Pareto frontier between stereotypical bias and personalization in the target setting (speech-implicit). Higher is better throughout. 4 BASIS-Bench Evaluation Models are eligible for our benchmark evaluation if they (1) support speech input, (2) accept textual instructions alongside speech, and (3) produce textual responses. We evaluate the following speech LLMs: audio-flamingo AF-3 and AF-Next [ 22 , 21 ] , DeSTA2.5 [ 32 ] , MOSS-Audio [ 48 ] , Qwen2.5- and Qwen3-Omni [ 46 , 47 ] , Step-Audio2 [ 44 ] , and Voxtral [ 31 ] . Figure 2 and Appendix Table 7 summarize the three axes and four evaluation modes. Appendix Tables 8 , 9 and 10 provide additional details for demographic robustness (§ 4.1 ), stereotypical bias (§ 4.2 ) and personalization (§ 4.3 ) axes respectively. 4.1 Demographic Robustness Results Acoustic Effect Most models perform robustly on content-based tasks (ASR/SQA) across demographic groups, with DeSTA2.5 showing the largest degradation on accented audio (Appendix Table 8 ). For classification, we observe that gender is considerably easier than age, with most models achieving high gender classification accuracy. Exceptions include Voxtral for male and Step-Audio2 for female speakers in BASIS-Health/Product, although the latter performs well on Spoken StereoSet+, suggesting dataset-dependent behavior. Age classification is harder. AF-Next and MOSS-Audio struggle with young adults, while AF-3, DeSTA2.5, Qwen2.5-Omni, Step-Audio2, and Voxtral struggle with elderly speakers. Child speakers also challenge DeSTA2.5 and Voxtral, but elderly speakers remain harder overall. Notably, Qwen3-Omni substantially improves over Qwen2.5-Omni on both elderly and child classification, suggesting better age perception. These measurements help isolate the acoustic effect when interpreting stereotypical bias and personalization, distinguishing failures to perceive demographic cues from how they are used. 4.2 Stereotypical Bias Results Figure 2 presents mean ICAT scores, while Appendix Table 9 reports per-demographic behavior. An ICAT score of 100 corresponds to perfectly balanced (50/50) stereotypical and anti-stereotypical selections across test samples. Backbone Effect text-implicit captures baseline behavior without demographic information, while text-explicit isolates the effect of providing speaker demographics to the backbone. Under text-implicit , some models slightly prefer female stereotypical continuations and, symmetrically, anti-stereotypical male ones. For age, behavior is more balanced, with only two models slightly favoring anti-stereotypical continuations for elderly speakers. Making demographics explicit ( text-explicit ) substantially increases stereotypical selections, especially for female and elderly speakers, though selections also rise for male and young speakers. Notably, the prompt does not instruct models to condition on the demographic attribute shared, yet models systematically incorporate it in a way that reinforces stereotypes. Qwen3-Omni, MOSS-Audio, and Voxtral exhibit the strongest bias across gender and age, while Step-Audio2 is particularly biased for gender. Characterizing these textual priors isolates stereotypical behavior inherited from the LLM from that arising through speech integration. Interaction Effect Comparing speech-explicit with text-explicit and speech-implicit with text-implicit reveals whether speech amplifies or dampens backbone disparities. In explicit mode, speech generally reduces stereotypical behavior relative to text. For gender, text-explicit produces more stereotypical continuations than speech-explicit , except for AF-3 and AF-Next (male), and MOSS Audio (female), all with small differences ( ≤ \leq 1.1). Age follows a similar pattern, except for AF-Next, MOSS-Audio and Qwen3-Omni (elderly; 3.4/1/5.6), and Qwen2.5-omni (young; 0.6), where speech increases stereotypical selections. In implicit modes, gender shows no consistent trend: text-implicit is more stereotypical for male speakers in 5/8 models, while speech-implicit is more stereotypical for female speakers in 5/8. Age exhibits a clearer interaction effect: speech-implicit increases stereotypical selections for elderly speakers in all models except AF-Next (-0.5). On average, speech shifts stereotypical selections by +4/-3.2 points for elderly/young speakers, compared with +2.1/-1.4 for female/male speakers. Overall, equivalent speech and text conditions remain closely aligned, suggesting that stereotypical behavior is largely inherited from the backbone . Interaction effects are small, but more consistent for age in the implicit mode. Perfect vs. Imperfect Perception We contrast speech-implicit , where models infer speaker demographics, with speech-explicit , where they are provided in the prompt. In the center column of Figure 2 , the shift from hollow to filled circles shows that explicit demographics consistently increase stereotypical selections. 6 6 6 Reverse DeSTA2.5/Qwen3-Omni trends are aggregation artifacts: explicit mode shift male from anti- to stereotypical, increasing ICAT more than the decrease observed for female. Appendix Table 9 shows increases of 4.7/3.4 points in stereotypical selections for female/male speakers, versus 20.1/9.2 points for elderly/young speakers, with Qwen3-Omni showing the largest increases (32.2/21.0). More broadly, increased stereotyping under speech-explicit suggests that relatively balanced speech-implicit behavior may reflect limited ability to perceive and translate demographic cues into behavioral changes, rather than genuine fairness . Deaf or Unbiased? Demographic classification distinguishes limited reliance on demographic cues from failures to perceive them. For elderly speakers, MOSS-Audio and Qwen3-Omni classify well (96.3/88.1; Appendix Table 8 ), yet show little stereotypical behavior under speech-implicit (60.4/53.1; Appendix Table 9 ). Once age is explicit, however, they become the most biased (78.7/85.3). Conversely, AF-3 and Voxtral poorly classify elderly speakers (0/13.4) and appear balanced under speech-implicit (44.3/48.8). Under speech-explicit , however, Voxtral shifts strongly toward stereotypical selections (75.7), suggesting that its apparent balance partly reflects limited perception, whereas AF-3 remains balanced (54.2). For gender, classification is more reliable (95.2/83.2 on average for female/male speakers), yet the slight text-implicit asymmetry in stereotypical bias largely persists under speech-implicit , with a smaller shift than for age, suggesting demographic cues are not considered. Overall, apparently balanced speech-implicit behavior may reflect limited reliance on demographic information rather than limited perception, while stereotypical trends largely mirror backbone priors . 4.3 Personalization Results Figure 2 presents mean personalization accuracy. Appendix Table 10 reports per-dataset gender results. text-implicit measures preferences among age profiles or gender answers without demographic information. For age, we additionally report text-baseline , which captures default behavior without a specified response style, whereas text-implicit includes child/adult profiles and their preferences. Comparing the two reveals how default responses align with these profiles, distinguishing default behavior from personalization. Backbone Effect For gender, text-implicit reveals a puzzling preference for female personalization across backbones, despite the BASIS-Health/Product datasets providing equally probable options differing only in gender-specific content. This preference is stronger for BASIS-Health (77.9 on average) than BASIS-Product (58.5). As chance-level accuracy is expected in this setting, these results suggest an underlying backbone tendency toward female personalization. In contrast, text-explicit yields near-ceiling performance, supporting the dataset design and showing that gender personalization is straightforward when gender is provided textually. For age, text-baseline shows that most models default to more adult-like responses, while Qwen3-Omni is the most balanced. Under text-implicit , most models show no strong profile preference, although DeSTA2.5 and Qwen3-Omni lean toward the adult profile and AF-Next toward the child profile. text-explicit reveals the backbone’s personalization capabilities: child personalization is straightforward for all models but AF-3 (64.1%), whereas adult personalization remains challenging. Only DeSTA2.5, Qwen3-Omni and Voxtral exceed 77%, while AF-Next and Step-Audio2 perform worst (34.9/42.1%, respectively). Once age is explicit, models readily personalize toward children but remain substantially less effective at adapting toward adults. Therefore, models default toward adult but show no consistent profile preference under text-implicit , then, when age is explicit, they readily personalize toward children but remain substantially less effective for adults. Interaction Effect We assess the interaction effect by comparing speech-implicit with text-implicit . For gender, speech-implicit is highly asymmetric, with substantially higher accuracy for female than male speakers (Appendix Table 10 ). Female performance is largely driven by BASIS-Health (82.6 on average), compared with BASIS-Product (66.4), while male personalization remains poor on both datasets (51.1/31.9 for BASIS-Product/Health). This closely resembles text-implicit , both in overall trends and, for several models, absolute performance, suggesting that models largely reproduce backbone preferences rather than exploit demographic cues in speech. Thus, speech does not reliably induce behavioral adaptation from demographic cues despite high gender classification accuracy (Appendix Table 8 ). A different pattern emerges for age: no model successfully adapts to both age groups under speech-implicit , with speech instead consistently shifting responses toward the child profile. Relative to text-implicit , personalization accuracy increases substantially for child speakers (+61.1 on average), while decreasing for adults (-47.2). This effect is particularly pronounced for DeSTA2.5, Qwen2.5-Omni, Qwen3-Omni, and Voxtral, whose relatively adult-oriented backbone behavior shifts strongly toward the child profile under speech. Rather than speaker-aware personalization, this shift may reflect a modality-induced style preference: speech-oriented training favors conversational answers aligned more closely with the child than the adult profile. Thus, unlike gender, age exhibits a strong interaction effect, but one that does not reliably track speakers age. Perfect vs. Imperfect Perception Under speech-implicit , personalization remains asymmetric for both age and gender despite their contrasting classification performance: age classification is relatively weak, whereas gender classification is generally reliable. In both cases, personalization largely resembles the backbone behavior under text-implicit , suggesting that models make limited use of speech demographic cues. When gender is explicitly provided under speech-explicit , personalization rises sharply for both groups, with all models achieving high accuracy. Thus, models can personalize based on gender when it is directly available, but struggle to translate speech demographics into the intended adaptation. Age reveals a different pattern. Qwen2.5-Omni and Qwen3-Omni classify both adult and child speakers reasonably well (79.1/85 and 75.5/99, respectively), yet strongly favor the child profile under speech-implicit , yielding low adult personalization accuracy. Voxtral shows the same preference despite accurately classifying adults but not children (92.2/14.4), suggesting that this behavior is not reliably speaker-aware. Under speech-explicit , child personalization becomes nearly trivial for most models, whereas adult personalization remains considerably harder. The same asymmetry under text-explicit indicates that this difficulty is not solely perceptual, but also reflects limitations already present in the backbone. Stereotyped or Personalized? Taken together, our results reveal two fundamental limitations in how speech LLMs use demographic information. (1) Recognizing demographic information does not imply using it effectively . Models often fail to translate speech demographic cues into the requested personalization: gender behavior remains shaped by backbone preferences, while age induces a broad shift toward the child persona that does not reliably track the speaker’s age. Stereotypical behavior similarly mirrors backbone priors. Crucially, this pattern emerges both in models that classify demographics well and in those that do not, revealing a gap between demographic perception and its translation into behavior. (2) Models do not reliably distinguish when demographic information should shape their behavior . Personalization explicitly requests demographic-dependent adaptation, whereas stereotypical bias evaluates behavior when such adaptation is neither requested nor relevant. Yet the gender Pareto frontier in Figure 2 shows that less stereotypical models tend to personalize less, while stronger personalization coincides with more stereotypical behavior. Explicit demographic information under speech-explicit shifts this trade-off but does not change the behavior: personalization improves, yet stereotypical behavior increases. Age exhibits a similar but weaker trade-off that also becomes clearer when demographics are explicit. Thus, improving demographic perception alone is insufficient: models must learn when to use this information and when to turn a deaf ear to it. 5 Conclusion We introduced BASIS-Bench to jointly evaluate stereotypical bias and personalization in speech LLMs while disentangling the sources of disparities. Across eight models, our results show that perceiving demographic information does not imply using it appropriately. Demographic-dependent behavior often remains shaped by language model priors, and models struggle to ignore demographic information when it is irrelevant. These findings call for more multi-dimensional evaluations covering demographic perception and its use. Limitations Nature of Bias Our evaluation focuses on stereotypical bias, capturing only one form of representational bias and not intersectional bias. Similarly, while our demographic robustness axis evaluates disparities across groups, it does not characterize all their sources. A comprehensive evaluation requires datasets covering broader forms of bias. Gender Labels Our evaluation adopts a binary categorization of gender, distinguishing between male and female speakers. We acknowledge that this does not capture the diversity of gender identities and expressions. Following recommendations for using gender as a variable in NLP [ 27 ] , we make this categorization explicit and justify it by the requirements of our evaluation: it enables a controlled task isolating whether speech LLMs exploit gender-related information for personalization and stereotypical bias evaluation. We thus use these categories as an experimental abstraction rather than a comprehensive representation of gender. Demographic Inference Our evaluation assumes that demographic categories can be associated with speech samples. However, attributes such as gender and age cannot always be reliably inferred from speech, and acoustic cues may reflect perceived rather than self-identified characteristics. Our results therefore measure models’ use of demographic cues in speech, rather than their ability to determine speakers’ demographic identities. Accent Evaluation We evaluate accent only for demographic robustness and exclude it from the personalization and stereotypical bias axes. Defining appropriate personalization based on accent is challenging without making assumptions about a speaker’s linguistic background, preferences, or cultural identity. We leave accent-based personalization and bias evaluation to future work. Spoken StereoSet Manual Annotation Blodgett et al. [5] argue that annotators recruited through crowd-sourcing platforms may be detached from the intended measurement construct, potentially resulting in annotations that do not faithfully capture the target notion of bias. For the reannotation of Spoken StereoSet (Appendix A.1 ), a dataset that passed through two rounds of crowd-sourcing annotations, we chose to perform the annotation ourselves. This decision does not come without limitations. While it allowed us to consistently apply the proposed annotation criteria, it substantially reduced the diversity and number of annotators involved in the process. As all annotators were contributors to this work and shared the same annotation guidelines, the resulting labels may still reflect common assumptions or blind spots that differ from those of other populations. Future work could validate and refine our annotation protocol through larger-scale studies involving annotators from more diverse backgrounds. For age personalization, ELIP-Pair uses a friendlier and more playful tone for children and a professional and more expert tone for adults. This formulation captures only a coarse form of age-based personalization. Our evaluation therefore tests whether speech LLMs can exploit coarse age-related cues when instructed to personalize, rather than whether they can provide comprehensive age-aware personalization.
